# How Qt runs your code {#sec-runtime}

QML bindings, signals and threads all rest on a few mechanisms in Qt's core. Understand
these five and most of Qt's behavior stops being surprising.

## The event loop {#sec-event-loop}

A Qt application is one loop. `QGuiApplication::exec()` starts it, and it runs until the
app quits:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    W(["Wait"]) --> E["Events arrive<br/>input, timers, network"]
    E --> D["Deliver each<br/>to its object"]
    D --> H["Handlers emit signals,<br/>bindings update"]
    H --> R["Render the<br/>next frame"]
    R --> W
```

Every click, timer and update passes through this cycle, on the main thread, one at a
time. (Qt Quick draws the frame itself on a render thread, @sec-custom-items.) That has one big consequence: **code that blocks the loop freezes the whole app.** No
input, no animation, no repaint until your function returns.

```cpp
QThread::sleep(2);                                 // frozen for 2 s
QTimer::singleShot(2000, this, &Uploader::retry);  // keeps running
```

Never wait inside the loop. Let a timer or a signal call you back, and move slow work to
another thread (@sec-threads).

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [The event system](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/eventsandfilters.html)
:::

## Properties and signals: the reactive contract {#sec-properties}

A `Q_PROPERTY` with a `NOTIFY` signal is state that others can observe. Change the value,
emit the signal, and every QML binding that reads the property updates itself.

```{.cpp filename="CanvasStore.hpp"}
class CanvasStore : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_PROPERTY(bool snapShapes READ snapShapes WRITE setSnapShapes
               NOTIFY snapShapesChanged FINAL)

public:
    bool snapShapes() const { return m_snapShapes; }
    void setSnapShapes(bool snap)
    {
        if (snap == m_snapShapes)  // <1>
            return;
        m_snapShapes = snap;
        Q_EMIT snapShapesChanged();  // <2>
    }

Q_SIGNALS:
    void snapShapesChanged();

private:
    bool m_snapShapes = true;
};
```
1. No change, no signal. This avoids needless updates and binding loops.
2. Every binding on `snapShapes` re-evaluates.

Mark a property `CONSTANT` when it never changes, and `FINAL` so that QML tooling can rely on
its type.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp` ·
**Read more:** [The property system](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/properties.html)
:::

## Signals and slots {#sec-signals}

A signal announces that something happened, without knowing who listens. `connect()` wires
it to a receiver:

```cpp
connect(&m_canvas, &CanvasStore::edited,
        this, &SketchbookViewModel::saveOpenSketch);
connect(&m_canvas, &CanvasStore::edited,
        this, [this] { scheduleBackup(); });
```

Use member-function pointers, as above: the compiler checks that signal and slot fit. The
third argument of the lambda version, the **context object**, matters: when it is
destroyed, the connection ends, and the lambda runs in that object's thread.

::: {.callout-note}
## `Q_SIGNALS` and `Q_EMIT`
The template writes `Q_SIGNALS`, `Q_SLOTS` and `Q_EMIT` instead of `signals`, `slots` and
`emit`. The short forms are macros, and they break third-party headers that use those words
as names.
:::

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Signals and slots](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/signalsandslots.html)
:::

## Who owns an object {#sec-ownership}

A QObject can have a **parent**. When the parent is destroyed, it destroys its children.
Objects without a parent belong to whoever created them: a stack variable, a member, or a
`std::unique_ptr`.

```cpp
auto *timer = new QTimer(this);                       // the parent deletes it
auto translator = std::make_unique<QTranslator>();    // the unique_ptr deletes it
SketchStorage storage(dataDir);                       // the scope deletes it
```

Give every object exactly one owner. With two owners, such as a parent *and* a
`unique_ptr`, the parent may delete the object first, and the `unique_ptr` later deletes it
a second time and crashes.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Object trees and ownership](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/objecttrees.html)
:::

## Threads: hand work off, send results back {#sec-threads}

Each QObject belongs to the thread that created it. The GUI belongs to the main thread and
must only be touched there. Slow work, such as writing a file or parsing a large document,
runs on another thread and reports back with a signal.

```{.cpp filename="Storage.cpp"}
void Storage::save(QString path, Document document)
{
    QtConcurrent::run(&m_writer,                                  // <1>
        [path, document = std::move(document)] { writeJson(path, document); })
        .then(this, [this] { Q_EMIT saved(); });                  // <2>
}
```
1. The worker gets its own copy of the data, or data that nobody changes. Then it needs no
   locks.
2. With a context object, the continuation runs in that object's thread: back on the GUI
   thread.

For long-lived background work, such as a network connection, move a worker object to a
`QThread` and talk to it through signals. Qt Quick itself renders on a separate thread, too
(@sec-custom-items).

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/sketchbook/SketchStorage.cpp` saves on a one-thread pool, so writes keep
their order ·
**Read more:** [Threads and QObjects](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/threads-qobject.html),
[The eight rules of multithreaded Qt](https://www.kdab.com/the-eight-rules-of-multithreaded-qt/)
:::
